extracted.intended_audience: Patent examiners and patent practitioners performing 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter-eligibility analysis for nature-based product claims (USPTO context).
extracted.subtask_description: A USPTO worksheet to guide claim-by-claim subject-matter-eligibility (SME) analysis under 35 U.S.C. §101 for claims that may involve nature-based products, walking the examiner through claim construction, Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (judicial exceptions) including the 'markedly different characteristics' test for product-of-nature issues, and Step 2B (significantly more / inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: What did applicant invent? / Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification to determine what applicant invented and record it in Section I. Every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited; use a separate worksheet for each claim. The worksheet use is optional but recommended. If needed, clarify claim interpretation in the Office action record (for example: the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim is not directed to an abstract idea or nature-based product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention is a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B. If No (not one of the four categories), make a rejection as drawn to non-statutory subject matter and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record if a rejection is made under Step 2. If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and continue examination under the other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the claim directed to a product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature exception when the claim recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. For other exceptions, it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. Refer to the Subject Matter Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet, 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, July 2015 Update, and the court decisions chart for assistance. Choose A (no exception), B (streamlined analysis appropriate), or C (claim directed to an exception — proceed to further questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature: apply the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics test only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are 'product of nature' exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered by the courts when determining whether there is a marked difference include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype, including functional and structural characteristics; and structure and form, whether chemical, genetic or physical. Note that a process claim is not subject to the markedly different analysis for nature-based products used in the process, except in the limited situation where a process claim is drafted such that there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple.'). Apply the analysis limitation-by-limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim directed to a nature-based product: identify limitation(s), closest naturally occurring counterpart, and compare
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe a nature-based product; identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state; compare to determine whether the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete parts (a) (list the nature-based product limitations), (b) (identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart), and (c) (explain comparison and select (i) The nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics (and thus is not a product of nature exception) with reasons; or (ii) The nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics (and thus is a product of nature exception) with reasons). Proceed thereafter to analyze whether the claim is directed to another type of exception (Question 2) or to Step 2B if an exception is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify limitations that recite an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, and/or natural phenomenon, identify the claim limitation(s) that recite the exception and explain why the recited subject matter is an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the limitation(s) and the reason(s) they are considered a judicial exception. Examples given: laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles or substances; abstract ideas include fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. Use the case law chart and 2014 Guidance for examples and alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident and a full eligibility analysis is not needed, a streamlined analysis may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use streamlined analysis (Choice B) when the claimed invention, as explained in Section I, is not focused on an exception and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an exception such that others cannot practice it. Refer to the February 2015 Training Slides for examples of streamlined analyses. If using streamlined analysis, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are there any additional elements beyond the exception(s)? (Step 2B.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claim recites additional elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the judicial exception(s) identified in Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that if the claim is directed to a product of nature comprising a combination of component elements that do not occur together in nature as claimed, each component element should be considered as an additional element to the other components to determine whether their combination results in significantly more. Choose 1 (No additional elements — conclude SME analysis with §101 rejection) or 2 (Yes — list additional claim elements and continue). If no additional elements, make a §101 rejection and consider whether there are elements in the disclosure that could be added to make the claim eligible (identify and suggest them to applicant). Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements to determine 'significantly more' / 'inventive concept' (Step 2B.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for an 'inventive concept' by considering whether the additional elements: improve another technology or technical field; improve the functioning of a computer itself; apply the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; not merely 'apply it'); effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; add a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at high-level); add unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); add meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Keep in mind what applicant invented (Section I) when evaluating significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion and Office action / sample rejection language
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude SME analysis based on whether additional elements amount to significantly more; prepare rejection or continue examination accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any elements, individually or as a combination, amount to significantly more than the exception(s), conclude SME analysis and continue examination under each of the other patentability requirements; clarify the record as needed (e.g., explain why the claim with additional element 'y' amounts to significantly more than the product of nature 'x'). If no elements amount to significantly more, conclude the SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with examination under other patentability requirements. Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. The worksheet provides sample rejection wording: 'Claim __ is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim __ is directed to _____. The claim does not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because _____.' Also, identify and propose elements from the disclosure that could be added to the claim to attempt to make it eligible.
